Subject: Request: topology + explanation for Dedicated/Private airlock pattern

Hi Marissa,

Following up from our SIG questionnaire review: Veridian's audit team needs a concise topology and a brief explanation of the 'airlock handshake' pattern Redwood uses for customers choosing Dedicated or Private deployments. Specifically, the auditor asks for:

- A network diagram showing the handshake surface between customer transit (VPC/VNet) and Redwood's enclave for both Dedicated and Private modes.
- A short narrative (1 page) that explains how the handshake enforces egress controls, KMS boundary, and emergency rundown/eviction.
- Any artifacts that demonstrate the controls (example diagrams, matrix of traffic flows, and an appendix with minimal steps to validate during an on-site or remote audit).

Could you send an initial package and, if possible, a short recording or 30-min call to walk the auditor through it? We're aiming to close the SIG/CAIQ questions this quarter.

Requested attachments: requested_network_sketches_v1.png, dataflow_matrix_v1.csv

Thanks,
--
Jordan Lee
Compliance Lead, Veridian Health
audits@veridianhealth.com

Subject: Re: Request: topology + explanation for Dedicated/Private airlock pattern

Jordan —

Thanks for the clear ask. We've pulled together an initial draft package attached (airlock_handshake_draft_v1.pdf). Short summary below and proposed next steps.

High-level summary (draft):
- Pattern name: "airlock handshake" — an intentional two-stage boundary where (1) customer-managed transit terminates at a constrained ingress/egress gateway, and (2) Redwood's enclave enforces a tightly scoped service front door. The handshake consists of mutually authenticated peering (or customer-to-provider transit) + a short-lived control-plane token exchange to ensure session provenance.
- Dedicated vs Private differences:
  - Dedicated: Redwood provides a reserved pool with a thin managed transit interface; customer traffic reaches a dedicated ingress subnet and Redwood enforces tenant fencing at the hyperplane with strict egress ACLs.
  - Private: Customer deploys Redwood runtime into their VPC/VNet (private control plane) with an optional air-gapped edge. The handshake is mediated by customer-controlled transit and an HSM-backed token exchange.
- Controls emphasized for auditors: KMS separation (customer KEKs vs Redwood KEKs), egress allowlist enforced at the ingress gateway, and an eviction procedure (isolating tenant compute and zeroing caches).

Attachments in this draft: airlock_handshake_draft_v1.pdf (topology, flows, glossary).

Next steps I propose:
1) Short call — 30 min to walk the draft (I can do 8/17 or 8/18).
2) If that looks good, we will add a 1-page auditor appendix that lists minimal validation steps and sample evidence points.
3) Kim and Rishi: I'll pull in your notes and add the KMS appendix and egress proof points.

Thanks — attaching the draft now.

Best,

Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com
Attachment: airlock_handshake_draft_v1.pdf (diagram + narrative)

Marissa / Jordan —

Good start. A few technical clarifications auditors always look for — I'll call them out here so we don't have back-and-forth: 

1) Egress control: please ensure diagrams explicitly show the egress choke point (managed NAT or proxy) and list the telemetry/log sources we can hand to the auditor (flow logs, proxy allowlist logs, per-connection principal).

2) KMS boundary: separate the diagrams for KEK ownership (customer-managed vs Redwood-managed) and include a short note on key rotation frequency and HSM attestations for Private installs. That tends to satisfy the deeper CAIQ questions.

3) Minimal validation steps: auditors prefer short, numbered steps. Suggest we add an "Auditor Appendix" with 6-8 concrete checks (ping endpoints disallowed, trace a session ID through the handshake, request KMS policy snapshot). I'll draft that appendix (kms_boundary_note.md & auditor_appendix_min_steps.docx).

4) Evidence packaging: include a link to a scrubbed flow log sample and a sanitized topology with hostnames redacted. That saves time in the next round.

If you want, I can drop these as tracked comments in the PDF and update the attachments.

K

Kimberly Park
Director, Security Architecture, Redwood Inference
kimberly_park@redwood.com
Attachment: kms_boundary_note.md (internal draft), auditor_appendix_min_steps.docx
